[PATH:empirical] Optogenetic manipulation of feedback projections to V1 combined with laminar recordings of gamma-band LFP and spike timing during ambiguous visual stimuli (e.g., Rubin's vase or binocular rivalry) in non-human primates — Directly tests causal role of feedback spike phase-locking to local gamma by perturbing feedback timing and measuring changes in perceptual disambiguation, providing empirical confirmation or refutation of the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of cortical microcircuits with conductance-based neurons and gamma oscillations, systematically varying the precision of feedback spike timing relative to gamma phase while simulating ambiguous feature integration — Allows controlled testing of whether phase-locking (vs. sub-millisecond precision) is necessary for resolving local feature conflicts, isolating the mechanism from confounding variables present in vivo.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of published studies on feedback to V1 during perceptual ambiguity, focusing on reported correlations between gamma-band phase coherence and perceptual switches (e.g., from electroencephalography or local field potential recordings in humans) — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether phase-locking of feedback is consistently observed during ambiguous reasoning, identifying gaps or conflicting results that support or undermine the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of recurrent cortical circuits with variable feedback delays — A spiking neural network model of V1 with feedback from higher areas can systematically vary feedback timing precision and measure its impact on disambiguating overlapping stimuli, providing a theoretical basis for whether sub-millisecond precision is required.

[PATH:empirical] Electrophysiological recordings of feedback latency variability in primate visual cortex during binocular rivalry — Existing literature on binocular rivalry and other ambiguous visual tasks often reports feedback latencies on the order of milliseconds; re-analyzing these data for correlation between feedback jitter and perceptual resolution could support or refute the need for sub-millisecond precision.

[PATH:empirical] Two-photon calcium imaging of V1 excitatory and inhibitory populations in mice performing an ambiguous visual discrimination task with spatially overlapping gratings, manipulating feature conflict and prior strength via optogenetic perturbation of higher-order feedback (e.g., from higher visual areas or prefrontal cortex). — Directly measures whether coarse gain modulation (e.g., uniform changes in firing rate) is sufficient to resolve ambiguity under high conflict or weak priors, or whether more complex feedback dynamics (e.g., feature-specific tuning shifts or divisive normalization) are required.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of recurrent cortical circuits with hierarchical Bayesian inference, comparing models that implement coarse gain modulation (e.g., simple multiplicative scaling) versus those with structured feedback (e.g., predictive coding or attractor dynamics) in their ability to disambiguate overlapping stimuli under varying conflict and prior strength. — Provides a formal test of sufficiency: if coarse gain modulation alone cannot account for behavioral or neural data under high conflict or weak priors, the hypothesis is supported; if it can, the hypothesis is refuted.

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review of electrophysiological and psychophysical studies on visual disambiguation (e.g., binocular rivalry, structure-from-motion, or figure-ground segregation) that report feedback-related neural signatures (e.g., gamma-band coherence, laminar profiles) and relate them to gain modulation versus feature-selective feedback. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether coarse gain modulation has been empirically sufficient in prior studies with similar ambiguity, conflict, and prior conditions, or whether additional feedback mechanisms are consistently implicated.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling with spiking neural networks that incorporate temporally heterogeneous feedback (e.g., with distinct axonal conduction delays or synaptic kinetics) and systematically lesioning sub-millisecond versus millisecond-range connections. — Allows controlled simulation of the hypothesized causal dependency, testing whether disambiguation fails only under sub-millisecond feedback removal, and can be validated against the existing simulated evidence.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of existing in vivo and in silico studies on feedback timing in visual cortex, focusing on studies that have measured or manipulated conduction delays or synaptic latencies in feedback pathways during perceptual tasks. — Provides a basis for assessing whether the sub-millisecond specificity is plausible given known biophysical constraints and whether any prior work inadvertently supports or contradicts the hypothesis.
